what: Making the taker's limit binding, so probing costs a fill. Predicted before it was built.
the_problem: A taker can submit requests it never intends to trade on and read the winning quote each time, mapping the price envelope for free. is_real cover traffic hides which slots are real from the MAKER; it does nothing about a taker that is the one asking.
the_proposal: The taker commits to an acceptance condition L along with the request. The circuit computes the winner q as it does now, then one more comparison, fill = (q <= L), and reveals q only when fill is set. A fill is binding: the quorum signs a zkPI that DeFMI settles against collateral the taker escrowed in advance, so there is no step at which the taker can decline.

the_information_argument.today: each request returns q, so a probe yields up to value_bits of information about the price envelope and costs nothing.
the_information_argument.with_a_binding_limit: fill = 0 returns exactly ONE BIT --- q > L --- and no trade. fill = 1 returns q and a trade.
the_information_argument.the_asymmetry_that_matters: A prober can raise L from below and learn q > L each time, for free, converging on q from underneath to any precision it likes. What it cannot get for free is an UPPER bound: learning that the market is BETTER than L requires being filled at it.
the_information_argument.so_the_honest_claim_is_not_that_probing_: It is that the free direction is 'the market is worse than I hoped', which is what not trading tells you in any market, and the costly direction is 'the market is better', which is a trade.
the_information_argument.binary_search_costs_fills: Bisecting for q terminates on the first answer of q <= L, which is a fill. Against a uniform q the first midpoint probe fills with probability 1/2, so a prober cannot bisect without trading about half the time. Only the linear crawl from below is free, and it needs range/step requests --- which a venue can rate-limit or price.
the_information_argument.the_ceiling_this_reaches: A resting limit order in a public book says exactly the same thing: I will trade at L, and not being filled says the market is worse. So a binding-limit RFQ leaks no MORE than a central limit order book, and less, because L is committed rather than displayed. run_clob_baseline.py already measures that baseline.

predictions.quantity: circuit cost of the fill gate
predictions.predicted: +2 to +8 rounds and under 0.5 percent traffic
predictions.arithmetic: one extra comparison against the tournament's existing log2(M) layers, plus one committed input and a multiplication to gate the output. The quote circuit is 70 rounds at M=16, and one LTZ is a few of them.

predictions.quantity: what the taker sees on a no-fill
predictions.predicted: nothing beyond the bit. Revealing fill and fill*q + mask means a no-fill hands back the taker's own mask, which it already knows.
predictions.note: the venue sees a uniform value either way, which it already does

predictions.predicted: NO, and any claim that it does would be wrong. It prices probing. A crawl from below stays free; anything that learns the market is better than a stated level costs a trade.

predictions.quantity: what it costs an honest taker
predictions.predicted: the right to decline after seeing the price --- which is 'last look', the practice the FX Global Code spent years constraining because it is what makes probing possible in the first place. Giving it up is aligned with where the regulation went, and it is a real cost: a binding limit is exposed to being filled on a stale quote, which is what the 26-second staleness measurement is about.

what_it_does_not_address: A Sybil taker with many identities, each probing once. But each identity has to escrow collateral and each fill is a real trade, so the cost still scales with the information taken --- which is the property being bought.
